Crowdsourced Cyclospora Watch

Crowdsourced Cyclospora Watch

Last updated: September 19, 2026 at 06:00 AM UTC

Feeling sick or have a confirmed case of cyclospora? Submit your report here

167 responses collected so far. This is a self-reported, crowdsourced tracker built to try to spot patterns in the current multistate cyclospora outbreak — not an official CDC or state health department investigation. There is no control group, so results below are proportional reporting among people who got sick, not proof of cause. Treat this as “worth watching,” not “confirmed.”

How certain is it that these are cyclospora cases?

The form asks everyone why they believe they have cyclospora. 27 of 167 responses (16.2%) are lab confirmed. Another 124 (74.3%) are self-suspected — people who have the symptoms and think they have it, without a test.

Every number on this page is computed over all 167 responses, including the self-suspected ones. That is deliberate. Excluding them would discard most of the data and bias what remains toward whoever was able to get a stool test — which is a function of healthcare access, not of what someone ate. But it does mean the leads below describe a mostly self-diagnosed population, and that is a real limit on how far any of them should be pushed.

Free-text answers here are counted, never quoted — some mention unrelated medical conditions. “Unclassified” means an answer didn’t clearly fit any tier, not that it was discarded.

Data Tables

Table 1: Produce Signal Ratio (Full Data)

CI columns are a 95% confidence interval — small sample sizes mean wide ranges. If the “Ratio CI low” column is still above 1, that’s a stronger lead than the point estimate alone.

Where these baselines come from

The signal ratio divides how often cases report a food by a baseline — how commonly people eat it normally. That denominator drives every number in this table, so it’s worth being explicit about where it comes from.

Of the 27 foods below, 15 have a baseline sourced from USDA ERS and 12 rest on the author’s own estimate. Both are labeled in the “Baseline source” column.

  • Author estimates are exactly that — considered guesses, not measurements, and not derived from any survey. They carry a pale ±30% band on the chart above to show roughly how much the ratio would move if the guess were off by that much. The band is one flat width for every estimate; pretending to know which guesses are shakier than others would be false precision.
  • USDA ERS values come from the Food Availability (Per Capita) Data System, refreshed monthly into baselines-external.json.

The ERS column is shown but not yet used, and the reason is a real limitation rather than an oversight. ERS publishes pounds of food available per person per year; the baseline this ratio needs is the share of people who ate a food in a two-week window. Those measure different things and cannot be converted into one another — 19 lb of tomatoes a year could be everyone eating a little or a few people eating a lot. Substituting one for the other would change every ratio on this page for no reason but a change of units. Reconciling them properly is open work; until then both numbers are shown side by side so the gap is visible rather than hidden.

Reported, but not yet rankable

A signal ratio needs a denominator, so a food with no baseline can’t appear in the table above. That’s 34 of the 61 foods reported so far — not a rounding error, and previously they simply vanished from the page with nothing said. They are listed here instead.

Two different reasons a food is on this list, and they need different fixes:

  • Ordinary produce with no baseline yet — lettuce_unspecified, onions, grapes, cherries, apples and the like. These could be ranked; they just need a “how often does a normal person eat this” number added to category_vocabulary.json. Adding one moves the food straight into the table above. lettuce_unspecified is the largest by some way, and the most worth doing: it is lettuce whose type the checklist recorded but whose form it didn’t, so it is ordinary produce rather than an unrankable composite.
  • Foods no per-capita figure can describe — dishes and composites like tacos, sushi, beef_burger or veggie_tray, and non-answers like no_specific_item. There is no meaningful “percent of people who ate a taco in a two-week window” to divide by, and inventing one would manufacture a ranking rather than measure it. These stay here permanently, which is the honest outcome, not a gap waiting to be filled.

lettuce_untyped is deliberately on this list too: it held the obsolete flat baseline of 55 while its siblings divide by 10–20, which published a signal ratio of 0.04 for what is otherwise a real lead. Removing the baseline was the fix.

Table 7: Stores & Restaurants Mentioned

Table 8: Reported Symptom Duration

Cyclospora illness tends to run longer than most foodborne bugs (often weeks, sometimes relapsing). Short-duration reports are more likely something else.

How to read this page: a high signal ratio means the food is reported by sick people more than you’d expect from normal eating habits — that’s a lead worth watching, not a verdict. Small numbers (a food only 2-3 people mentioned) are noisy and easy to over-read. If something looks concerning and consistent, the right next step is reporting it to your local or state health department, who can do formal case-control interviews and trace product lots — this page can’t do that part.
